Q233219.title: Second Battle of Ypres
paras: The Second Battle of Ypres, fought from 22 April to 25 May 1915 in the Ypres Salient in Flanders, Belgium, was the first battle in which poison gas was used on a large scale. By 1915 the Western Front had settled into trench warfare, and the German army looked to gas, promoted by the chemist Fritz Haber, to break the deadlock. The salient around Ypres bulged into the German lines, which held higher ground on three sides. It was held by French, British and Canadian troops: the French 45th (Algerian) Division and a territorial division on the northern face, the 1st Canadian Division, recently arrived and about to see its first major action, beside them, and British divisions to the right.

Late on 22 April, after the wind had delayed the attack for weeks and again that day, the Germans opened cylinders dug into their front line and released a cloud of chlorine over the French and Algerian trenches. Parks Canada and Veterans Affairs Canada put the gas at about 160 tons; EBSCO's account says over 400 tons. The French troops died or fled, leaving a gap in the Allied line that Veterans Affairs Canada puts at 6.5 kilometres. Warnings from aerial reconnaissance and German deserters had been ignored. The Germans, who had planned only a limited, experimental attack and had no reserves ready, advanced a few kilometres and dug in.

Through the night the Canadians fought to close the gap and counter-attacked at Kitchener's Wood near St. Julien, at heavy cost. On 24 April the Germans released gas again, this time against the Canadian line; the Canadians held on, breathing through wet cloths, despite rifles that jammed, until British reinforcements arrived and on 25 April allowed a fighting withdrawal. The breach was eventually sealed, and the rest of the battle became a contest of attrition. Later the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry held Bellewaarde Ridge at heavy cost, and the battle ended on 25 May.

In about 48 hours of fighting, 6,035 Canadians, one in three of the division, became casualties, and more than 2,000 died, according to Veterans Affairs Canada; Parks Canada gives about 6,000 casualties. Most of the battle's dead were killed by artillery and machine guns rather than gas, but gas had a heavy effect on morale, and the Allies soon developed gas weapons of their own. The Canadians' stand earned them a reputation as formidable soldiers, and in the battle's aftermath John McCrae wrote 'In Flanders Fields'.

Q324916.title: Battle of Solferino
paras: The Battle of Solferino, fought on 24 June 1859 near the Mincio river in northern Italy, was the decisive battle of the Second Italian War of Independence between the Austrian Empire and the allied armies of France and Piedmont-Sardinia. Piedmont's prime minister Count Cavour had won French support for a war to drive Austria out of northern Italy; France's price was Nice and Savoy. When Austria sent Piedmont an ultimatum in April 1859, France came in on Piedmont's side. After their defeat at Magenta, the Austrians abandoned Lombardy and fell back towards their fortresses on the Mincio, and Emperor Franz Joseph took personal command of his army.

Three monarchs led their armies in person, which is why the battle was also called the Battle of the Three Sovereigns: Napoleon III and King Victor Emmanuel II on the allied side and Franz Joseph on the Austrian. Estimates of their strength differ: EBSCO gives the allies some 118,600 men and the Austrians about 120,000, while HistoryNet puts the Austrian army at 100,000. Poor scouting on both sides made it a chance encounter: Napoleon III believed the Austrians were still retreating and ordered an attack, while the Austrians, who had no reserves, were surprised by the allied advance.

The allies advanced early in the morning, and through the long day the French made repeated, poorly coordinated attacks on the hills held by the Austrians, often carrying positions only with the bayonet, while the Austrians replied with costly counter-attacks. The French slowly pushed the Austrian centre and south back. In the north the Piedmontese attacked the corps of Ludwig von Benedek again and again but could not break it. In the late afternoon Franz Joseph ordered a retreat across the Mincio, covered by Benedek's corps.

Losses were heavy: about 22,000 on the Austrian side and about 17,000 for the allies, some 5,500 of them Piedmontese, though the breakdown differs between sources. Napoleon III, shaken by the carnage, sought a separate peace, and at Villafranca in July he agreed to a settlement under which Austria ceded Lombardy, passed through France to Piedmont, but kept Venetia, to the anger of Cavour and other Italian patriots; France gained Nice and Savoy. A Swiss businessman, Henri Dunant, who saw the wounded after the battle and organised local people to help them, wrote 'A Memory of Solferino', which led to the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva in 1863 and the first Geneva Convention.

Q722699.title: Fashoda Incident
Q722699.place: Fashoda, on the White Nile in the Sudan
paras: The Fashoda Incident of 1898 was a confrontation between Britain and France at Fashoda, a derelict fort on the White Nile in the Sudan, that brought the two countries to the brink of war. It grew out of their rivalry in Africa. Britain controlled Egypt and wanted the Sudan, then held by the followers of the Mahdi's successor, the khalifa, to link its territories along the Nile; France, still resentful of the British hold on Egypt, hoped for a belt of territory across Africa from west to east and, by seizing the upper Nile, a hand on Egypt's water.

A small French expedition under Captain Jean-Baptiste Marchand, made up of French officers and Senegalese soldiers, set out eastward from the French Congo, carrying even the parts of a steamboat across central Africa, and reached Fashoda on 10 July 1898. Meanwhile the British general Herbert Kitchener led an Anglo-Egyptian army up the Nile to reconquer the Sudan. After defeating the khalifa's forces at Omdurman, he went on to Fashoda on the orders of the prime minister, Lord Salisbury, with gunboats and a far stronger force, arriving on 18 or 19 September. The two commanders met courteously, raised their flags over different parts of the fort, and left the decision to their governments; Kitchener claimed the whole Nile valley for Britain.

In both countries the press and public opinion called for a firm stand. The French foreign minister, Théophile Delcassé, saw that France's position was hopeless: Kitchener was far stronger on the spot, Britain's navy dominated the Mediterranean, and France wanted British support against Germany. Under steady British pressure, France ordered Marchand to withdraw on 3 November 1898. According to EBSCO, in March 1899 France gave up all claims along the Nile in return for territory in the Sahara; one encyclopedia speaks of a guarantee of its position in West Africa.

Fashoda marked the high point of Anglo-French tension in Africa. Instead of war, it became part of the process that brought the two countries together: in 1904 they signed the Entente Cordiale, and in 1914 France went to war against Germany as Britain's ally.

Q4411.title: Battle of Valmy
paras: The Battle of Valmy, fought on 20 September 1792 near the village of Valmy in the Argonne region of north-eastern France, was the first important engagement of the French Revolutionary Wars and stopped the Prussian-led invasion of France. Revolutionary France had gone to war with Austria earlier in 1792, and an Austrian and Prussian army under the Duke of Brunswick crossed the frontier and marched towards Paris; Brunswick issued a manifesto threatening Paris with destruction if the royal family were harmed. The fortresses of Longwy and Verdun fell with little resistance, and in Paris fears of treason fed the September Massacres of prisoners.

The French generals Charles-François Dumouriez and François Christophe Kellermann, recently appointed, had to fill out and equip armies made up of regular soldiers and new volunteers. Dumouriez first planned to hold the Argonne forest, but the Austrians forced a pass and outflanked him; he regrouped around Sainte-Menehould and called Kellermann to join him. Bad weather slowed Brunswick's advance and allowed the two French armies to unite. They took position on the plateau of Valmy, by a windmill, with the Prussians placed on the Paris side of them. Hérodote gives 47,000 French against 34,000 Prussians.

When the fog lifted in the early afternoon, Kellermann raised his hat on his sword and shouted 'Vive la Nation!', and his troops took up the cry. The Prussian infantry began an assault on the windmill but fell back under French artillery fire, and for the first time in the war the French stood their ground. Brunswick did not press the attack, and the day became mainly an exchange of artillery fire, halted inconclusively by heavy rain; it showed the superiority of the French artillery. According to Hérodote, fewer than 500 men were hit in all, about 300 French and 184 Prussians.

Brunswick, now outnumbered, withdrew towards the Rhine; the retreat began the next day, and Hérodote says the last invading troops left France in late October. The modest cannonade had an outsized effect across Europe, showing the unexpected strength of the revolutionaries, and in November Dumouriez went on to defeat the Austrians at Jemappes and take Brussels. The German poet Goethe, who witnessed the cannonade, wrote some thirty years later that he had said there and then that a new epoch of world history was beginning.

Q1417059.title: First Fitna
paras: The First Fitna (656-661) was the first civil war within the Muslim community. It was fought between the supporters of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, who became the fourth caliph; the partisans of the murdered caliph Uthman, first led by Muhammad's widow Aisha with Talha and Zubayr and then by Mu'awiya, the Umayyad governor of Syria; and, from 657, the Kharijites, who broke away from Ali. It ended the Rashidun Caliphate and brought the Umayyads to power.

Uthman had been accused of favouring his Umayyad relatives, and discontent over provincial revenues and his appointments grew into open revolt: rebels from Egypt and Iraq marched on Medina and killed him in June 656. Ali was then recognised as caliph, but his accession was clouded by the unpunished murder. Aisha, Talha and Zubayr demanded vengeance and a new election, took Basra and were defeated by Ali outside the city on 8 December 656 in the Battle of the Camel, named after the camel of Aisha around which her forces rallied; Talha and Zubayr were killed.

Mu'awiya, Uthman's kinsman, refused to recognise Ali and went to war in the name of revenge for Uthman. The two armies met at Siffin on the Euphrates in 657 (Wikipedia: fighting from 26 July; EBSCO: August). When the battle turned in Ali's favour, the Syrians raised copies of the Quran on their lances to call for arbitration, and Ali, under pressure from his own troops, agreed. The arbitrators, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali and Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiya, reached no lasting settlement, but their proceedings strengthened Mu'awiya, whom the Syrians then accepted as caliph. Those of Ali's followers who rejected arbitration, saying judgment belonged to God alone, became the Kharijites; Ali crushed them at Nahrawan, while in 658 Amr took Egypt for Mu'awiya.

In January 661 the Kharijite Ibn Muljam assassinated Ali in the Great Mosque of Kufa. His eldest son Hasan was proclaimed caliph in Kufa, but as Mu'awiya marched on Kufa and Hasan's forces suffered widespread defections, Hasan made peace and recognised Mu'awiya, beginning the Umayyad Caliphate. EBSCO's account notes that the war temporarily held back the Arab conquests and laid the basis for the lasting rift between Sunni and Shia Muslims.

Q167259.title: Battle of Lützen
Q167259.place: Lützen, south-west of Leipzig (Electorate of Saxony)
paras: The Battle of Lützen was fought on 16 November 1632 (6 November in the Julian calendar then used in Sweden and Protestant Germany) near the small town of Lützen, south-west of Leipzig in Saxony, during the Thirty Years' War. A Swedish army under King Gustavus II Adolphus, with German Protestant allies from Saxony and Hesse-Kassel, attacked the Imperial (Catholic Habsburg) army of Albrecht von Wallenstein. Gustavus had landed in northern Germany in June 1630 and won a run of victories, but in 1632 Wallenstein had checked him outside Fürth and then invaded Saxony to force its elector out of the war.

In mid-November Wallenstein began to send his troops into winter quarters and detached Pappenheim's corps to Halle. Learning of this, Gustavus advanced to attack; Wallenstein recalled his scattered forces and drew up a defensive line along the Lützen-Leipzig road, his right anchored on the town. Wikipedia puts Gustavus's army at about 19,000 against 13,000 to 15,000 Imperial troops before Pappenheim returned; EBSCO's Research Starter gives the Swedes 18,000. Fog delayed the Swedish attack, which Wikipedia says began at 11:00 and EBSCO at 8 a.m.

The Swedish infantry crossed the road and began to turn the Imperial left, but Pappenheim arrived with his cavalry around midday, drove them back and was himself mortally wounded. Leading an attempt to rally his men in the fog and smoke, Gustavus rode into an Imperial cavalry unit and was killed. The Swedes, under Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar and their other commanders, renewed the attack, took Lützen and the Imperial batteries, and at dusk Wallenstein withdrew, leaving guns and baggage; he then fell back into Bohemia. Casualty figures differ widely: Wikipedia gives about 6,000 Swedish and 5,160 Imperial killed or wounded, EBSCO about 10,000 Swedish and 12,000 Imperial, and the historian Peter H. Wilson writes that over a quarter of all the combatants were killed or seriously wounded in nine hours of fighting.

Most historians count Lützen as a Swedish victory, but the death of the king left the Protestant side without its leader. His six-year-old daughter Christina succeeded him and the chancellor Axel Oxenstierna kept Sweden in the war, while France took an ever larger part in the anti-Habsburg alliance. Wilson notes that the battle did not end the war or even mark a significant turning point, yet it is among its best-remembered battles because of Gustavus's death, which Swedish propaganda presented as a Protestant martyrdom; a stone marks the spot where he fell, and Sweden still commemorates him every 6 November.

Q168556.title: Schmalkaldic War
Q168556.place: Holy Roman Empire (Swabia, Saxony and Bohemia)
paras: The Schmalkaldic War of 1546-1547 was fought in the Holy Roman Empire between the Emperor Charles V, with his commander the Duke of Alba and the Lutheran Duke Maurice of Saxony as allies, and the Schmalkaldic League, the defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities led by Elector John Frederick I of Saxony and Landgrave Philip I of Hesse. Wikipedia dates it from July 1546 to May 1547; EBSCO's Research Starter gives June 1546 to June 1547. The bpb, Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, calls it the first German war of religion.

The League had been formed at Schmalkalden after the Diet of Augsburg of 1530 rejected the Protestant position (Wikipedia: in 1531). For years Charles was held back by his wars elsewhere, but peace with France in 1544 freed him to turn to Germany. With papal money and troops, he gathered an army from Spain, Italy, Germany and the Netherlands, secured the backing of Bavaria (EBSCO; Wikipedia says its duke declared himself neutral) and won over Maurice, John Frederick's ambitious cousin, who hoped to gain his cousin's lands and electoral vote. Publicly Charles said he was punishing disobedient rebels, and on 20 July 1546 he put John Frederick and Philip under the imperial ban; the bpb notes that privately he called it a matter of religion.

The League mobilised first, but its divided leaders failed to strike at the emperor or at his Tyrolean and Bohemian lands, and in the autumn the armies manoeuvred inconclusively in southern Germany. When Maurice invaded Electoral Saxony (Wikipedia: in October; EBSCO: in November), John Frederick hurried home, the League's army in the south broke up, and the southern Protestant cities and princes submitted to Charles. In spring 1547 Charles marched into Saxony with his Spanish veterans and on 24 April 1547 surprised and routed John Frederick's army at Mühlberg on the Elbe, taking him prisoner.

On 19 May 1547, in the Capitulation of Wittenberg, John Frederick gave up his electoral title and much of his land to Maurice; in June Philip of Hesse surrendered, trusting in promises of leniency, and was imprisoned. Charles then tried to impose a religious settlement close to Catholic doctrine, the Augsburg Interim of 1548, but it was widely resisted, and his treatment of Philip and his push for imperial power turned princes of both faiths against him. In 1552 Maurice led a new princes' revolt, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 gave Lutheranism legal recognition, showing the limits of the emperor's power.

Q172077.title: Dome of the Rock built
paras: The Dome of the Rock, an octagonal shrine on the Temple Mount (al-Haram al-Sharif) in Jerusalem, was built for the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik and is the oldest surviving major monument of Islamic architecture. A dedicatory inscription inside gives the year 72 AH, 691/2 CE, which most historians take as the year the original building was completed; later Muslim writers dated the start of work to 685/6 or 688. It stands over a rock outcrop, the Foundation Stone, near the centre of the esplanade where the Jewish Temple once stood.

Abd al-Malik had the work supervised by Raja ibn Haywa, a Muslim theologian, and by Yazid ibn Sallam and his son Baha, and employed skilled workers from Syria and Egypt, who were presumably Christians. The building is a low octagon whose arcades form two ambulatories around a central space about 20 metres across, covered by a high wooden dome. Its plan and its mosaics of trees, plants, jewels and vases follow late antique and Byzantine models, and it resembles in plan and dome size the nearby Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which is also raised over a rock; but its Arabic inscriptions and lack of human figures marked it out from contemporary Christian buildings.

Why Abd al-Malik built it is debated. He was at war with the Byzantines and with the rival caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who held Mecca. One medieval explanation, current by the ninth century, was that he meant to draw pilgrims away from the Kaaba while it was in enemy hands; both sources note that this view is widely doubted. The building's own inscriptions, the only contemporary evidence, do not mention Muhammad's Night Journey, later linked to the rock, but set out the nature of Islam and reject the divinity of Christ, which suggests it was meant to proclaim Islam as the successor to Judaism and Christianity.

The shrine was repaired many times. The Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun's name was put in place of Abd al-Malik's in the inscription, though the original date was left. After the dome collapsed in an earthquake (Wikipedia: 1015; the Encyclopedia of Islam and the Muslim World: 1016) the Fatimids rebuilt it. The Crusaders made it a church, the Templum Domini, and Saladin restored it to Muslim use after retaking Jerusalem in 1187; the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent replaced the outer mosaics with tiles in the sixteenth century.

Q465627.title: Sack of Rome, 1527
paras: On 6 May 1527 troops of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who was also king of Spain, stormed Rome and began a sack that lasted, in waves, until February 1528. The victims were the city and Pope Clement VII, who in 1526 had joined France, Milan, Venice and Florence in the League of Cognac to limit the emperor's power in Italy. The imperial army that had invaded northern Italy, Spaniards under Charles, Duke of Bourbon and German Landsknechte under Georg von Frundsberg, many of them Lutherans, along with Italian troops, had gone unpaid for a long time and was close to mutiny.

In March 1527 the pope agreed a truce with the imperial viceroy of Naples, Charles de Lannoy, but Bourbon's men refused to honour it, and the duke, who could not pay them, led them south against Rome and its riches; whether Charles V approved the attack is disputed. The army reached the walls on 5 May. Rome was weakly held: Wikipedia counts about 5,000 militiamen and 189 Swiss Guards. Bourbon was killed in the first assault on 6 May, by his own account by the goldsmith Benvenuto Cellini, but by evening the attackers had taken almost the whole city. The Swiss Guard was nearly wiped out covering the pope's escape along the raised passage to the Castel Sant'Angelo.

Bourbon's successor, Philibert, Prince of Orange, could not control the troops. For days they killed, raped, tortured citizens to make them reveal or pay money, and held people of every allegiance for ransom; churches, monasteries and palaces were plundered, relics were profaned, and German soldiers staged mock Catholic ceremonies, seating a prostitute in priestly robes on the throne of St Peter. Clement surrendered in June (Wikipedia: 6 June; the Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World: 5 June), agreeing to pay a large ransom, and was held in the Castel Sant'Angelo until December. Plague, hunger and the approach of a French-led League army finally made the occupiers leave in February 1528.

Wikipedia gives an estimated 6,000 to 12,000 people murdered and Rome's population falling from about 55,000 to 10,000; the EHNE encyclopedia counts at least 12,000 deaths, rising with hunger and disease. The sack is often seen as the end of the High Renaissance in Rome: artists and scholars left, spreading Roman culture elsewhere. Clement, without the means to resist, came to terms with the emperor and crowned him in Bologna in 1530. Across Europe the sack was read in religious terms, by Lutherans as the punishment of the papal 'Antichrist' and by many Catholics as a judgment on a corrupt Church.

Q51649.title: First Crusade
Q51649.place: From western Europe across Anatolia and Syria to Jerusalem
paras: The First Crusade (1096-1099) was the first of the religious wars launched by the Latin Church to bring Jerusalem and the Holy Land under Christian rule. Its starting point was a request for help from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, whose empire had lost much of Anatolia to the Seljuk Turks after their victory at Manzikert in 1071; his envoys appealed to Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza in 1095. At the Council of Clermont in France that November (EBSCO: on Tuesday 27 November 1095), Urban called on Christians to take up arms, and his hearers answered with the cry 'God wills it'. EBSCO's account adds that Urban hoped to heal the 1054 schism with the Eastern Church and to strengthen papal leadership of Christendom.

The first to respond were crowds of mostly poor people led by the preacher Peter the Hermit and the knight Walter Sans Avoir. On its way through Germany this People's Crusade attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland massacres, and after crossing into Anatolia it was destroyed by the Turks at Civetot (Wikipedia: October 1096; EBSCO: August 1096). The main armies of nobles, the Princes' Crusade, set out in late summer 1096 under leaders including Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Toulouse with the papal legate Adhemar of Le Puy, Bohemond of Taranto, and northern French and Flemish lords; no king took part. Wikipedia says the whole host, with non-combatants, may have numbered as many as 100,000.

At Constantinople most of the leaders swore to hand back to the Byzantines any former imperial lands they recovered. The crusaders and the Byzantines took Nicaea in June 1097 (EBSCO: on 19 June, the city being handed to the emperor), and the crusaders beat the Turks at Dorylaeum in July. After a hard march across Anatolia they besieged Antioch, which fell in June 1098 (EBSCO: 3 June) and was kept by Bohemond; they then defeated the relief army of Kerbogha, the atabeg of Mosul, outside the city. In June 1099 they reached Jerusalem, which the Fatimids of Egypt had recently retaken from the Seljuks, and stormed it on 15 July 1099, killing a large part of the population.

Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to lead in Jerusalem with the title Defender of the Holy Sepulchre, and a Fatimid counter-attack was beaten off at Ascalon later in 1099, which ended the crusade; most crusaders then went home. Urban II died on 29 July 1099, two weeks after the capture of Jerusalem. Four crusader states were set up, the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. EBSCO notes that the crusaders' success owed much to the political divisions of the Muslim world, and that once these were overcome new crusades were needed; the crusaders kept a presence in the region until the fall of Acre in 1291.

Q735876.title: Battle of Siffin
Q735876.place: Siffin, on the Euphrates near Raqqa (Syria)
paras: The Battle of Siffin was fought in 657 between the army of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph, drawn mainly from Iraq, and the Syrian army of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the Umayyad governor of Syria. It took place at Siffin, a ruined village on the right bank of the Euphrates near Raqqa in present-day Syria, and was the central battle of the First Fitna, the first Muslim civil war.

The war followed the murder of the third caliph, Uthman, by rebels in Medina in 656 and the election of Ali in his place. Mu'awiya, Uthman's kinsman and the head of the Umayyad clan, refused to pledge allegiance to Ali and demanded that Uthman's killers be punished first; some of Ali's supporters had been among the rebels, and Ali refused. In Syria, Uthman's bloodstained shirt was carried from town to town to rouse the people to revenge.

Ali's army reached Siffin early in the summer of 657 and found the Syrians holding the watering place; the Iraqis drove them off but let the Syrians use the water. For about three months the two armies, reluctant to shed Muslim blood, faced each other with skirmishes and negotiations. Wikipedia says the main battle can be dated with some certainty to Wednesday 26 July 657 and lasted until the Friday or Saturday morning, with fighting through a night remembered as laylat al-harir; EBSCO's Research Starter gives August 657. Among the dead on Ali's side was Ammar ibn Yasir, an elderly companion of the Prophet. As the battle turned in Ali's favour, Syrian soldiers raised pages of the Quran on their lances, calling for the Book of God to judge between the sides, and the fighting stopped.

Under pressure from most of his troops, Ali reluctantly accepted arbitration. An agreement signed on 2 August 657 named Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali and Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiya; their meetings in 658-659 settled nothing, but they strengthened Mu'awiya and weakened Ali. A minority of Ali's followers, who held that only God could judge, broke away and became known as the Kharijites. In January 661 a Kharijite killed Ali in the mosque at Kufa; his son Hasan gave up the caliphate to Mu'awiya, who founded the Umayyad dynasty. The battle is seen as a major step towards Umayyad rule, and EBSCO's account dates the lasting division between Sunni and Shia Muslims from this civil war.

Q836844.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
paras: The Battle of al-Qadisiyyah was fought between the army of the Rashidun Caliphate, sent by the caliph Umar under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and the army of the Sasanian Empire of Persia under its commander Rustam Farrokhzad, at the small town of al-Qadisiyyah where the Mesopotamian floodplain meets the desert, in what is now south-western Iraq. Its date is uncertain: Wikipedia gives November 636, with the fighting widely held to have begun on 16 November and to have lasted about three days and a night; the 2025 Antiquity study of the site gives AD 636/637 in its text and about 637/8 in its summary, and Archaeology magazine gives 636 or 637.

Arab Muslim forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid had overrun much of Sasanian Iraq in 633, but after Khalid was sent to Syria the Persians, recovering from years of civil war under the young emperor Yazdegerd III, struck back and defeated the Muslims at the Battle of the Bridge. Umar raised a new volunteer army from across Arabia and gave Sa'd the command. The Arabs camped at al-Qadisiyyah from July 636, and months of embassies, in which the Muslim envoys offered conversion to Islam, payment of the jizya tax or war, came to nothing. After the Byzantine defeat at the Yarmuk in August 636, veterans of that battle were sent on to Iraq; Wikipedia says 5,000 of them arrived on the second day of the fighting. Its article reports modern estimates of about 30,000 men on each side, while noting that most scholars think the Sasanian army was considerably larger.

Sa'd, ill with sciatica and boils, directed the battle from the old palace at al-Qadisiyyah through a deputy, Khalid ibn Urfuta. The Persians crossed to the west bank of the Ateeq, a branch of the Euphrates, and their war elephants led attack after attack, repeatedly throwing the Arab cavalry into disorder; the Muslims answered by shooting the elephants' riders and cutting their saddle girths, and on the third day by blinding the animals and cutting their trunks until they fled. The third day's fighting went on through the night, remembered in Muslim chronicles as the 'Night of Rumbling Noises'. On the last day Rustam was killed, in circumstances that the accounts tell differently, and the Sasanian front collapsed; the commander Jalinus got much of the army back across the bridge while Muslim cavalry pursued the rest.

The victory opened the way to the Sasanian capital, Ctesiphon, which Wikipedia says fell in March 637 after a two-month siege; a Persian counter-attack was later defeated at Nahavand, and the last Sasanian emperor, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651. The Antiquity study calls the battle decisive for the Islamic conquest of Mesopotamia, Persia and beyond, and of great cultural significance in the Arab world. In 2024 researchers from Durham University and the University of al-Qadisiyah identified the likely site from declassified 1970s US spy-satellite images and from historical texts on the Darb Zubaydah pilgrimage road, though the study says further archaeological work is needed to confirm the date of the remains.

Q467777.title: Battle of Wagram
Q467777.place: Marchfeld plain north-east of Vienna (Austrian Empire)
paras: The Battle of Wagram was fought on 5 and 6 July 1809 on the Marchfeld, the flat plain north of the Danube opposite Vienna, between Napoleon's French army, with its German and Italian allies, and the Austrian army of Archduke Charles. It was the decisive battle of the War of the Fifth Coalition, which Austria had begun that spring, and with some 300,000 men engaged it was the largest battle fought up to that time.

Napoleon had taken Vienna, but his first attempt to cross the Danube had ended in defeat at Aspern-Essling in late May. He spent six weeks preparing a second crossing, this time with well-built bridges from the island of Lobau, and fooled Charles into expecting him to land where he had landed before. On the stormy night of 4 July the French crossed further east and spread out across the plain. Charles held a strong position behind the Russbach stream and the low Wagram escarpment, and called on his brother Archduke John to march in from Pressburg to join his left. Napoleon's evening attacks on 5 July gained ground at first but were thrown back, amid confused fighting at the village of Deutsch-Wagram in which Saxon troops fired on each other in the dark.

At dawn on 6 July Charles attacked along the whole line, hoping to envelop the French. The attack on the French right failed, but on the left the Austrians retook Aderklaa and advanced almost to the Danube bridges. Napoleon sent heavy cavalry against the Austrian centre, moved Masséna's corps south to block the threat to his left, formed a great battery of guns, and sent Macdonald forward in a huge column that suffered terrible losses. The decisive blow came from Davout on the French right, who took Markgrafneusiedl and turned the Austrian left. With Archduke John still hours away, Charles ordered a disciplined retreat in the early afternoon, and the exhausted French could not pursue at once.

Losses were very heavy on both sides and are counted differently. Ian Castle, writing for the Fondation Napoléon, gives about 23,750 Austrian killed and wounded, 7,500 prisoners and some 10,000 missing, against about 27,500 French killed and wounded and 10,000 prisoners and missing; Wikipedia gives the official French figure as 6,901 dead and 26,757 wounded, and notes that an Austrian count found 51,626 men missing by 11 July, a figure that includes later actions. Among the dead was the French cavalry general Lasalle. Charles retreated north and, after the French caught him at Znaim, asked for an armistice. The Treaty of Schönbrunn that followed cost Austria about a sixth of its subjects and its access to the sea.

Q312492.title: Herero and Nama genocide
paras: Between 1904 and 1908 the German Empire destroyed much of the Herero and Nama peoples of its colony German South West Africa, today Namibia. Most historians now class it as genocide. German rule had brought forced land clearances and the loss of the grazing land and water on which the cattle-herding Herero depended, and the settlers treated Africans as second-class people with almost no rights; a cattle plague in 1896-97 had deepened their poverty.

On 12 January 1904 the Herero, led by Samuel Maharero, rose against the colonists, attacking farms and settlements, cutting railway lines and besieging German posts; Wikipedia puts the Germans killed at 123 to 160, and the Deutsches Historisches Museum's LeMO at over 120, most of them farmers and traders. The small colonial force was at first outmatched, but Germany sent about 14,000 troops, and in May 1904 General Lothar von Trotha took command, intending a war of annihilation.

In August 1904 Trotha's forces surrounded the Herero at the Waterberg (LeMO: battle on 11 August). Most of the Herero, largely women and children, fled into the Omaheke desert; German troops shot many, held or poisoned waterholes and sealed the desert edge with a cordon that the bpb puts at 250 km long, and thousands died of thirst and hunger. On 2 October Trotha proclaimed that every Herero found within the colony's borders, armed or not, would be shot, and that he would no longer take in women and children. After protests in Germany, from missionaries and from Chancellor Bernhard von Bülow, the order was withdrawn in December. Survivors were then held in concentration camps and used for forced labour; Wikipedia says around half of the prisoners died there. The Nama, who rose against the Germans in the autumn of 1904 (Wikipedia: September; bpb: October), were also crushed. The camps were closed in 1908.

The death toll is uncertain. Wikipedia gives 40,000 to 80,000 Herero (about 80 percent of the people) and 10,000 Nama (about half); the bpb says only about 16,000 of 60,000 to 80,000 Herero survived and about half of some 20,000 Nama died; LeMO says between a third and two thirds of the Herero died by the end of the state of war in March 1907. In 2004 the German development minister Heidemarie Wieczorek-Zeul asked the descendants for forgiveness at Okakarara, and in 2015 the German Foreign Office called the war a genocide. Wikipedia reports that a 2021 agreement with Namibia offered 1.1 billion euros in development aid while denying legal responsibility, a deal rejected by most Herero and Nama organisations.

Q917435.title: July Crisis
Q917435.place: Vienna, Berlin, Belgrade, St Petersburg, Paris and London
paras: The July Crisis was the month of diplomatic and military escalation among the great powers of Europe in the summer of 1914 that turned a quarrel between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into the First World War. Wikipedia dates its beginning to 28 June 1914, when the Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip assassinated the Austro-Hungarian heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo; the event is placed here at 23 July, the day of Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia.

There were grounds to suspect that Serbian officers were behind the plot, and leaders in Vienna wanted a military blow against Serbia, both to show Austria-Hungary's strength and to weaken the Yugoslav nationalism that threatened its multi-national empire. Fearing that Russia would defend Serbia, Vienna first sought German backing. In early July Emperor Wilhelm II and Chancellor Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg promised to stand by their ally in a war against Serbia; this promise became known as the 'blank cheque' (Wikipedia gives both 5 and 6 July as its date). According to LeMO, Germany did not want to lose its last ally, and its leaders also saw the conflict as a test of the alliance system.

After weeks of deliberation, Austria-Hungary, in close agreement with Germany, handed Serbia a 48-hour ultimatum on 23 July with demands meant to be unacceptable, including Austro-Hungarian involvement in investigations on Serbian soil. Serbia's reply, which historians judge differently, did not accept every demand, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July, rejecting further mediation by the other powers. Russia began mobilising in support of Serbia; Wikipedia says the Tsar ordered general mobilisation on 30 July, while LeMO dates Russia's mobilisation against Austria-Hungary to 29 July. On 31 July Germany demanded that Russia stop within 12 hours.

When Russia did not, Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. Its war plan required a rapid advance through neutral Belgium, and Britain, citing the invasion of Belgium, declared war on Germany on 4 August. Within a few days a local Balkan conflict had become a general European war; LeMO notes that in every country most people believed the war had been forced upon them by their enemies.
claims: The July Crisis was a series of diplomatic and military escalations among the major European powers in mid-1914 that led to the First World War; Wikipedia: it began on 28 June 1914.

Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo (LeMO: 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo).

There were grounded indications of Serbian (intelligence) involvement in the plot (LeMO; Wikipedia: Potiorek reported on 5 July that Serbian Major Tankosić had directed the assassins); Austro-Hungarian politicians and military pressed for a military strike against Serbia.
Wikipedia: Austria-Hungary wanted to demonstrate its strength and dampen Serbian support for Yugoslav nationalism, a threat to its multi-national empire; fearing Russia, it sought German support.

Bethmann Hollweg and Wilhelm II promised in early July to support Austria-Hungary in a war against Serbia (LeMO); this was the 'blank cheque' (Wikipedia, which dates it 6 July in one passage and 5 July in another).
LeMO: Germany did not want to lose Austria-Hungary as its last ally; the war was to be a test case for the alliance system.

On 23 July Austria-Hungary, in close agreement with Germany (LeMO), gave Serbia a two-day ultimatum (Wikipedia: reply due by 6 p.m. on 25 July) whose demands were deliberately unacceptable (LeMO; Wikipedia: a harsh ultimatum Serbia was certain to reject), including freedom for investigations in Serbia.
Historians disagree on how far Serbia's reply compromised (Wikipedia); Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July after rejecting further mediation by the other powers (LeMO).
Russian mobilisation: Wikipedia, partial mobilisation ordered on 28 July and general mobilisation on 30 July; LeMO, Russia mobilised against Austria-Hungary on 29 July.
On 31 July Germany demanded that Russia halt its mobilisation within 12 hours (LeMO; Wikipedia: ultimatum delivered near midnight).
Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August (Wikipedia, LeMO).

Germany's plan required an advance through neutral Belgium; Britain entered the war on 4 August, citing the invasion of Belgium (LeMO; Wikipedia: Germany declared war on Belgium on 4 August; Britain entered the war on 4 August).
LeMO: within days the conflict became a general European war; because of nationalism and propaganda most people in all states believed the war had been forced on them by enemy states.

Q12989672.title: Coup of 9 Thermidor
Q12989672.place: Paris: the National Convention and the Hôtel de Ville
paras: On 9 Thermidor Year II of the revolutionary calendar, 27 July 1794, the National Convention in Paris turned against Maximilien Robespierre, under whom, in EBSCO's account, the Committee of Public Safety had directed the Terror, and had him arrested with his closest allies; within two days he and scores of his followers had been guillotined, and the Reign of Terror came to an end. The men who brought him down were themselves members of the revolutionary government and deputies, among them Tallien, Fouché, Barras and Billaud-Varenne, acting together with the moderate deputies of the Convention.

By mid-1794 Robespierre had purged the Girondins, the Hébertists and Danton's followers, and the law of 22 Prairial (10 June 1794) let the Committee have any suspect arrested and executed. In a speech of about two hours to the Convention on 8 Thermidor (26 July) he threatened a league of 'rogues' without naming them. Every deputy who might feel threatened, especially those who had enriched themselves or committed atrocities as representatives on mission, had reason to strike first, and they organised during his absences from the Committee and the Convention.

When the session of 9 Thermidor opened, Tallien and Billaud-Varenne interrupted Saint-Just's speech with accusations, and Robespierre was shouted down when he tried to speak. The deputies Louchet and Loiseau obtained the arrest of Robespierre, his younger brother Augustin, Saint-Just, Couthon and Le Bas. The Paris Commune proclaimed an insurrection, and its supporters freed the prisoners, who gathered at the Hôtel de Ville; but Robespierre's side gave no clear orders, and the Convention outlawed the rebels and called on the moderate Paris sections. At about 2 a.m. troops led by Barras broke into the Hôtel de Ville. Robespierre was wounded in the jaw by a pistol shot; Larousse says he had tried to kill himself.

On the evening of 10 Thermidor (28 July) Robespierre was guillotined with Saint-Just, Couthon and his brother; Larousse counts 22 executed that day and 71 on the next, Hérodote about twenty and then some 80. The victors, called the Thermidorians, freed suspects and ended the Terror, beginning the 'Thermidorian reaction', which led in 1795 to a new constitution and the Directory.

Q750567.title: Spring Offensive
Q750567.place: Western Front in northern France and Flanders
paras: The German Spring Offensive of 1918, also called the Kaiserschlacht ('Kaiser's Battle'), was Germany's last great attempt to win the First World War on the Western Front, launched against the British and French armies from 21 March 1918. Russia's withdrawal from the war had freed large numbers of German troops for the west, and the German command, under General Erich Ludendorff, knew that submarine warfare had failed to defeat Britain and that American troops would soon arrive in strength. It aimed to break through, split the British from the French and take the railway centre of Amiens; the Australian War Memorial notes the view that Ludendorff no longer expected outright victory but wanted a stronger position for peace talks.

The first blow, Operation Michael, fell south of Arras around St Quentin on the British Third Army under Byng and Fifth Army under Gough. The Fifth Army held a long front with few divisions and weak defences in depth. After a five-hour 'hurricane' bombardment (the National Army Museum counts around 10,000 guns firing over a million shells; National Records of Scotland 6,500 guns and 3,500 heavy mortars), storm troops helped by fog infiltrated the weak points and broke through. National Records of Scotland puts British losses on the first day at 38,500, of whom 21,000 were captured. The figures given for the attackers differ: the NAM says 47 German divisions attacked, the AWM 63 divisions against 26 British.

Within five days, the Australian War Memorial says, the Germans retook all the ground lost on the Somme in the two previous years and came within a few miles of Amiens. On 26 March the Allies placed the French Marshal Foch in overall command, and Australian divisions were rushed in to block the road to Amiens at Villers-Bretonneux. Exhausted and short of transport, the Germans called off Michael on 5 April. A second attack, Georgette, began south of Ypres (NAM: 7 April; National Records of Scotland: 9 April), retook the Messines ridge and much of the Passchendaele salient, and prompted Haig's 'backs to the wall' order before it too lost momentum.

Further offensives against the French followed from 27 May to 17 July, but Germany had exhausted its army. On 18 July the French counter-attacked on the Marne, and on 8 August the British attack at Amiens, which Ludendorff called 'the black day of the German Army', began the Allies' 'Hundred Days', a series of offensives that drove the Germans back until the ceasefire ended the war. The National Army Museum says the mobile fighting since March had cost each side over a million men.

claims: The German Spring Offensive / Kaiserschlacht began with Operation Michael on 21 March 1918 against the British (NAM, AWM, NRS).
NAM: Russia's withdrawal released German troops; the Germans knew submarine warfare had failed and that large numbers of American troops would soon arrive (AWM: US forces about to arrive).

Aims: AWM, Ludendorff planned to divide the French and British, capture Amiens and weaken the Allies; it is generally accepted Ludendorff did not by then expect to win the war and aimed at a stronger position at peace negotiations; NRS: to separate the British from the French and force the British back to the Channel.
Michael fell south of Arras in the St Quentin sector (AWM) on Byng's Third and Gough's Fifth Armies (NAM, NRS).

The Fifth Army held a long front with few divisions (NAM: 14 divisions for 67 km) and weak defences in depth (NRS); bombardment of five hours (NAM: around 10,000 guns, over a million shells; NRS: 6,500 guns and 3,500 heavy mortars); storm troops infiltrated weak points (NAM, NRS; NRS: helped by fog).
NRS: British first-day casualties of 38,500, of whom 7,000 killed and 21,000 captured.
Attacking forces: NAM 47 German divisions; AWM 63 German divisions against 26 British; NRS 43 divisions against the Fifth Army and 19 against the Third.
AWM: in five days the Germans retook all the ground lost on the Somme in the previous two years and came close to Amiens; NRS: the Germans were only five miles from Amiens by the end of March.
NAM: on 26 March Haig agreed to Foch's appointment as supreme commander; AWM: Australian divisions were sent from 25 March to stop the advance before Amiens at Villers-Bretonneux.
The Germans, exhausted and short of transport, halted (NAM: by 5 April held east of Amiens; NRS: called off Michael on 5 April).
Operation Georgette, south of Ypres: NAM 7 April, captured the Messines ridge and much of the Passchendaele salient; NRS 9 April (Battles of the Lys); NAM quotes Haig's 'backs to the wall' order.
NAM: offensives against the French between 27 May and 17 July; on 18 July the French counter-attacked on the Marne; Germany had exhausted its army.

NAM: on 8 August Rawlinson's Fourth Army attacked at Amiens; Ludendorff called it 'the black day of the German Army'; it began the Hundred Days, a series of offensives that drove the Germans back, until the ceasefire came into effect and ended the war.

Q170360.title: Armistice of 22 June 1940
paras: On 22 June 1940, six weeks after the German invasion of France began on 10 May, the French government of Marshal Philippe Pétain signed an armistice with Nazi Germany in the Forest of Compiègne. The agreement was signed at 6.50 p.m. by General Wilhelm Keitel, chief of the German armed forces high command, and by a French delegation led by General Charles Huntziger that included the former ambassador Léon Noël. According to Hérodote, Hitler insisted on holding the ceremony at Rethondes in the very railway carriage in which the German delegates had signed the armistice of 11 November 1918, in order to wipe out that humiliation, and he sat in the place Marshal Foch had occupied before leaving the negotiators to their work.

The terms cut France in two. German troops would occupy the north and west of the country, including the Atlantic coast, while a zone south of a line from the Swiss border near Geneva to the Spanish border was left unoccupied; the French government could sit there or in Paris. In the occupied zone Germany held all the rights of an occupying power, and French officials had to cooperate with the German commanders. The French army, navy and air force were to be demobilised and disarmed, apart from forces needed to keep order, and the fleet was to be laid up in its ports under German or Italian control, Germany declaring that it would not use the ships for its own war. France also had to pay the costs of the German occupation.

Other articles bound France to hand over on demand any Germans in its territory named by the German government, a clause that, according to Hérodote, General Weygand protested in vain as a betrayal of the word given to political refugees and German Jews; French citizens who fought on for another country against Germany were to be treated as insurgents; and French prisoners of war were to stay in captivity until a peace treaty. Hérodote counts about 60,000 French soldiers killed in the campaign and 1.85 million taken prisoner, more than a million of whom remained in Germany for four years.

The agreement could take effect only once France had also made an armistice with Italy, and fighting was to stop six hours after Italy notified Germany of it; Hérodote gives the moment as 0.35 a.m. on 25 June 1940. Hérodote adds that leaving part of the country unoccupied was meant to dissuade the French leaders from setting up a government in exile. The armistice was to last until a peace treaty, and Germany could end it at any time if France failed in its obligations.

Q665554.title: Japanese Instrument of Surrender
paras: On 2 September 1945 Japan formally surrendered to the Allies in Tokyo Bay, ending the Pacific war and with it the Second World War; Germany had surrendered four months earlier. The Instrument of Surrender was signed, according to Hérodote on the deck of the American battleship Missouri, by Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu on behalf of the Emperor and the Japanese government and by General Yoshijiro Umezu, chief of the army general staff, on behalf of the Imperial General Headquarters. It was accepted by General Douglas MacArthur as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and by representatives of the United States (Admiral Chester Nimitz), China, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, Australia, Canada, France (General Leclerc) and other Allied nations.

In the document Japan accepted the terms of the Potsdam Declaration, issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, China and Britain and later joined by the Soviet Union, and proclaimed the unconditional surrender of the Imperial General Headquarters and of all Japanese armed forces wherever they were. Japanese forces and people were ordered to stop fighting at once and to preserve ships, aircraft and property; Allied prisoners of war and civilian internees were to be freed and cared for; and the authority of the Emperor and the Japanese government to rule was placed under the Supreme Commander.

The surrender followed months of defeat after the destruction of Japan's fleet at Midway, the dropping of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945, and the Soviet declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria on 9 August. Hérodote argues that the collapse of the Japanese army in Manchuria and the fear of a Soviet invasion weighed more with Japan's leaders than the atomic bombs. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced his decision to end the war, heard over loudspeakers in the streets; it was the first time his subjects had heard his voice.

A formal peace treaty was signed only on 8 September 1951 in San Francisco, by Japan with the United States and 47 other Allied nations; the Soviet Union and the People's Republic of China did not sign. Under it, Hérodote notes, Japan recognised the independence of Korea and gave up its claims to the Kurile Islands, Sakhalin and Taiwan.
